messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T20

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T20 Distributed energy storage (and microgrid power management)

## 0. What is being rated, and two problems with the inputs

**Scope disagreement.** Claude frames T20 as storage hardware. GPT adds "microgrid power management". I rate the two separately because they sit at different TRLs:

- **T20-S:** site storage, 0.5–15 MWh usable.
- **T20-R:** robot packs, 10–50 kWh.
- **T20-P:** the MW-class 1–3 kV DC microgrid that ties together storage, site arrays, plant loads and tether-fed robots.

The headline range below covers all three. Folding T20-P in lowers the floor by about one level. That choice belongs to the panel.

**Stale related RQs.** rq-0-21 and rq-0-22 concern a 100 MW, $500M III-V array at L4/L5 feeding a central Processing Station. The revised architecture (D-01) abandoned that design. Neither RQ, nor the attached literature review, is evidence for T20. I would not reuse that review's numbers without checking them. For example, its "$100–300/cm²" cell cost looks roughly an order of magnitude high against per-watt space-cell pricing, though I have not verified current prices. Only rq-0-60 (tether insulation) bears on T20, through the robot power interface.

**The requirement is under-defined, which caps the rating.** Three things are still TBD: discharge power, recharge profile and outage duration (GPT). Claude's 9,000–33,000 cycles assume surface-sited arrays. Those cycle counts are consistent with an NEA rotation period of about 4–10 h over 10–15 yr, i.e. about 900–2,200 cycles/yr. I have not seen the derivation.

Night length is roughly half the rotation period, about 1–5 h for P = 2–10 h. The arithmetic follows:

| Case | Load | Night | Energy needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep-alive (BMS, thermal, comms, robot standby) | 0.1–0.3 MW | 1–5 h | 0.1–1.5 MWh |
| Full process ride-through | 2.5–8 MW | 1–5 h | 2.5–40 MWh |

So 15 MWh covers full ride-through only for fast rotators and low plant power. The 0.5–15 MWh range therefore spans two different operating philosophies: nightly curtailment versus partial ride-through. Neither has been chosen.

**Mass consequence.** Installed capacity equals usable capacity divided by depth of discharge (DoD). Assumptions: pack-level specific energy 100–150 Wh/kg (my estimate for space-grade packs, not verified), and DoD that falls as cycle count rises (about 60% at ~9k cycles, about 25% at ~33k cycles).

- Low end: 0.5 MWh at 60% DoD and 150 Wh/kg gives about 6 t.
- High end: 15 MWh at 25% DoD and 100 Wh/kg gives about 600 t, and roughly 700 t with enclosures and thermal control.

The high end exceeds one tug payload (150–300 t). That is why the 200–500 MWh bank was abandoned, and the same logic bites at 15 MWh if arrays are surface-sited and the plant runs through the night.

**The requirement depends on the metallurgy route.**

| Route | Effect on storage |
|---|---|
| Claude (no-melt: magnetic beneficiation → carbonyl or H₂ reduction) | Lower process temperatures; probably tolerates nightly curtailment. Pushes storage toward the low end. |
| Gemini (rotating smelting furnace) | A furnace cannot be cheaply thermally cycled every 1–5 h. Needs hot standby or ride-through. Pushes toward the high end, or toward thermal rather than electrical storage. |
| GPT (gated native-metal production) | Intermediate; depends on which experiment passes. |

## 1. Evidence

| # | Claim | Source | Demonstrated scale / environment | Ratio (required ÷ demonstrated) | Confident? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | NiH₂ batteries delivered roughly 19 yr of LEO service (on the order of 10⁵ eclipse cycles) at shallow DoD | Hubble Space Telescope, 1990 launch; batteries replaced on SM4, 2009 | ~10 kWh class (6 batteries; capacity figure from memory), LEO, thermally controlled inside spacecraft | Cycles: ≤1. Energy: ~50–1,500× | Duration: yes. Energy figure: no |
| E2 | Li-ion ORUs replaced the NiH₂ batteries on ISS; MW-scale cycling heritage in LEO with propagation-resistant design | ISS battery replacement, EVAs 2017–2020 (GS Yuasa cells, Aerojet Rocketdyne / Boeing) | Aggregate on the order of 10² kWh (exact figure not verified), LEO, ~16 cycles/day | Site energy ~2–100×; cycles ≤1 | Programme: yes. Aggregate kWh: no |
| E3 | Daily-cycled Li-ion on a planetary surface for more than a decade, under thermal cycling and dust | MSL Curiosity (2012–); Mars 2020 Perseverance (2021–). Two Li-ion batteries of ~42–43 Ah each, MMRTG-charged | ~2–3 kWh per rover. Mars atmosphere, not vacuum | Robot pack ~4–20× | Programme: yes. Ah figure: mostly |
| E4 | Dust on radiators degraded battery thermal control on a surface vehicle | Apollo 15–17 Lunar Roving Vehicle (silver-zinc primary batteries). Reported in Apollo mission reports; I cannot cite the specific document | ~kWh, lunar vacuum and dust, days | n/a (a failure-mode precedent, not capability) | No |
| E5 | MWh–GWh Li-ion BESS with microgrid / grid control is commercial | e.g. Vistra Moss Landing (~3 GWh class; major fire January 2025) and many others | ≫15 MWh, terrestrial, air-cooled, 1 g | <1 in scale. Environment entirely different | Yes (existence and fire). Capacity: approximately |
| E6 | Spacecraft DC microgrid with storage, switching and fault isolation | ISS EPS: 160 V primary / 120 V secondary DC, ~100 kW class, remote power controllers | ~0.1 MW, 160 V, LEO | Power ~25–80×; voltage ~6–19× | Yes |
| E7 | High-voltage solar arrays in space plasma suffer ESD and sustained secondary arcing | GEO array failures, late 1990s; e.g. Hoeber et al., AIAA, 1998 (I believe this is the relevant paper but have not checked the exact reference) | ~100 V-class arrays, GEO | Failure-mode precedent for 1–3 kV | Phenomenon: yes. Citation: no |
| E8 | Long-cycle Li-ion (LFP / NMC) cycle-life data at partial DoD | Manufacturer datasheets and academic ageing studies | Cells, lab, 15–45 °C | n/a. Supports a life model, not space use | Yes (as a class; I cite no specific paper) |

**What is not evidence.**
- Lunar surface power and Fission Surface Power design studies.
- The panel's agreement that "distributed storage replaces the bank".
- Any flown regenerative fuel cell or flywheel at relevant scale. The ISS flywheel energy storage effort did not fly, to my knowledge.

## 2. Current TRL

| Element | TRL | Met at lower bound | Unmet for next level |
|---|---|---|---|
| T20-R robot packs, 10–50 kWh | **4–5** | TRL 4: space Li-ion cells and modules validated, with lab test data agreeing with models. TRL 5 can be argued from E3, but E3 is at 4–20× smaller scale and not in vacuum. | TRL 5 → 6: no 10–50 kWh pack has been tested in vacuum, at NEA diurnal thermal profile, with regolith-dust radiators and a tether-loss ride-through. Scaling requirements are undocumented. |
| T20-S site storage, 0.5–15 MWh | **4–5** | Cells and modules are flight-proven (TRL 9 at kWh–100s kWh in LEO). Cycle count is met in LEO at shallow DoD (E1, E2). | TRL 5 exit, "documented definition of scaling requirements", is unmet. Siting, DoD, outage case and discharge power are TBD, and the scale ratio is ~2–100×. No space MWh assembly with thermal enclosure, propagation control and NEA-surface thermal design exists. |
| T20-P 1–3 kV, 2.5–8 MW DC microgrid with tethered loads | **3–4** | TRL 3: terrestrial MVDC and microgrid control with test data; ISS EPS at 160 V and 0.1 MW. | TRL 4 exit: "documented definition of the relevant environment" is unmet. Plasma, outgassing, charged regolith and arc thresholds at 1–3 kV are undefined (rq-0-60 pending). No breadboard at kV in vacuum. |

**Headline: TRL 3–5.**
- The floor is set by T20-P and by the missing environment and requirements definition. This is a requirements gap, not a physics gap.
- The ceiling is set by the cell and module heritage.
- I do not rate T20-S at 6 on the grounds that "cells are flight-proven and the rest is paralleling". Three things are new and not parallel:
  - thermal control on an NEA surface with ~150–400 K swings and dust on radiators;
  - fault propagation at 10–100× ISS energy;
  - BMS and protection at kV.

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Risk classification.** T20 is not project-ending if a fallback exists (see §5), so D-02 does not mandate TRL 6 at KDP-0B.

**Targets.**
- **0A internal milestone (0A mid-term review):** TRL 4 for all three elements. This includes a documented relevant environment and a sizing case per metallurgy route.
- **KDP-0B:** TRL 5 for T20-S and T20-P; TRL 6 for T20-R, which the pathfinder can demonstrate.
- **Before 0B deployment / PDR:** TRL 6 for T20-S and T20-P.
- **Timing assumption:** the inputs give no KDP-0B date. I assume about 5–7 years after D-01, i.e. roughly 2031–2033.
- **Condition:** if the panel adopts surface-sited arrays plus Gemini's continuous furnace as the reference, the classification moves toward project-ending and the KDP-0B target should become 6.

**AD² = 4** (new development; similar development has been done, ≈80%).
- Storage chemistry, cycle life and BMS are within the experience base (AD² 3 on their own).
- Integration at MWh and 1–3 kV in vacuum, with tether-fed robots and dusty radiators, is similar in kind to ISS EPS and terrestrial MVDC but has not been done in this environment. That lifts the rating to 4.
- I would rate 5 if the high-end case (15 MWh at ≥30k cycles) becomes the reference, because the mass closure is then unproven.

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Requirements closure:** surface vs stand-off arrays; rotation-period envelope of candidate targets; curtail vs ride-through per metallurgy route; outage and tether-cut cases; discharge power; thermal vs electrical storage for furnace hot standby | Analysis | Site-level | 0.2–0.8 M | 0.5–1 yr | Enables TRL 4 (environment and scaling defined) |
| 2 | **Life-model literature and data mining:** Hubble and ISS battery data, LEO fleet data, LFP/NMC partial-DoD ageing at 0–30 °C; combined calendar and cycle model | Literature | Cell | 0.1–0.3 M | 0.5 yr | Supports TRL 4 |
| 3 | **Accelerated cycle-life test** at the DoD from step 1, cycling at the profile from step 1 (1–5 h nights). Real-time 33k cycles at a 4 h period takes 15 yr; even 90-min LEO-style cycling takes ~5.7 yr. **Start early in 0A** and accept extrapolation from partial data | Experiment | Cells and small modules, hundreds of cells | 1–4 M | 2–6 yr (interim data at ~2 yr) | TRL 4 → 5 (cycle-life element) |
| 4 | **TVAC module test:** ~50–200 kWh module with enclosure, heaters, radiator loaded with regolith simulant, and the NEA diurnal profile | Experiment | 1/10–1/100 of site storage | 3–10 M | 1.5–3 yr | TRL 5 (T20-S) |
| 5 | **Robot pack qualification:** 10–50 kWh pack through TVAC, vibration, dust, charging transients, and a tether-cut ride-through with the tether interface from rq-0-60 | Experiment | Full scale | 2–6 M | 1–2 yr | TRL 5–6 (T20-R) |
| 6 | **Vacuum HV arc and Paschen tests** at 1–3 kV with charged simulant (shared with rq-0-60) | Experiment | Components | 1–3 M | 1–2 yr | TRL 4 (T20-P) |
| 7 | **Ground hardware-in-the-loop microgrid testbed:** 1–3 kV DC at 0.5–1 MW (subscale of 2.5–8 MW), with storage, a simulated diurnal array, tethered robot loads and fault protection (solid-state breakers) | Experiment | 1/3–1/16 of site power | 10–30 M | 2–4 yr | TRL 5 (T20-P) |
| 8 | **Pathfinder demonstrator power subsystem:** storage plus one tether-fed robot in space or at the NEA. Cost is incremental to the pathfinder | Experiment | kWh–tens of kWh (MWh remains extrapolated by ~10–100×) | 20–60 M | 3–6 yr | TRL 6–7 for T20-R; partial 6 for T20-S and T20-P (scale gap remains) |
| 9 | **Alternative storage trade:** sensible thermal storage (e.g. Fe-Ni or regolith thermal mass) for furnace standby; regenerative fuel cells only if the water pilot exists | Analysis plus bench | Subscale | 0.5–2 M | 1–2 yr | TRL 3–4 for the alternative |

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: architecture-change.** If storage at the needed scale and cycle life does not close in mass, the architecture changes along one of these lines:

- Move arrays off the surface (stand-off or co-orbiting). Cycle count then falls to contingency events, and the storage drops to fault and outage ride-through. This creates a new transmission technology to rate.
- Accept nightly curtailment. This favours Claude's no-melt route and penalises Gemini's furnace.
- Restrict target selection to fast rotators.
- Substitute thermal storage for process heat.

If stand-off siting is already the reference, the class falls to **cost-increase**.

**Fallback:** size storage to keep-alive only (≤1.5 MWh), curtail processing every night, and select targets and metallurgy routes that tolerate curtailment. If that fails the KDP-0B economics gate, use D-02's pre-committed "0A only, Earth supply".

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Scope.** GPT's inclusion of microgrid power management sets the floor at TRL 3. A storage-only rating would be TRL 4–5. Both views should stay on record.
2. **"It's TRL 6 already."** One can argue that Li-ion is TRL 9 and MWh is just paralleling. I reject this on scale ratio (~2–100×), the NEA-surface environment and fault propagation. A reasonable assessor might rate T20-S at 5.
3. **Risk class.** Gemini's continuous-furnace route, with surface arrays on a slow rotator, makes storage close to project-ending. My architecture-change rating assumes curtailment or stand-off is acceptable.
4. **The cycle requirement.** Claude's 9k–33k figure is conditional on surface siting. If the panel assumes stand-off arrays, the binding requirement becomes outage energy and power, not cycles, and the high-end mass problem largely disappears.
5. **The mass figures.** These are my arithmetic, not data. The 100–150 Wh/kg space pack range and the DoD-versus-cycles assumption are both contestable by roughly ±30–50%.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence

- **ISS Li-ion Battery Upgrade (2017–2021):** The ISS replaced its Ni-H2 batteries with 24 Li-ion Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs). Each ORU has a nameplate capacity of ~9.7 kWh and is designed for ~60,000 LEO charge/discharge cycles over 10 years. This perfectly matches the 10–50 kWh per robot requirement and exceeds the 9,000–33,000 cycle requirement.
- **ISS Power Management System:** Manages ~120 kW of distributed solar power and storage. 
- **Terrestrial Microgrids (e.g., Tesla Megapack):** 1–15 MWh storage and MW-class power management are commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) on Earth, but have never been packaged for or tested in a space vacuum/thermal environment at this scale.

Scale ratio: Robot batteries (1:1). Site storage (15 MWh required vs ~0.3 MWh ISS, ratio 50:1). Power management (8 MW required vs 0.12 MW ISS, ratio ~65:1).

### 2. Current TRL

**TRL 3–4.** 
The core battery chemistry and 10–50 kWh packaging are TRL 9 (ISS). However, the 0.5–15 MWh distributed space microgrid and MW-class space power management lack component/breadboard validation in a relevant environment. The lower bound (3) is met by analytical models of MW-class space power systems; the upper bound (4) is unmet because a MWh-class space-rated battery bank and MW-class microgrid controller have not been tested together in a vacuum chamber.

### 3. Target and difficulty

**Target:** TRL 6 by KDP-0B (needed for Phase 0B site power architecture).
**AD²:** 4. New development; similar development has been done (ISS power system, terrestrial MWh microgrids), but scaling space power management by 50x requires significant engineering for thermal dissipation and high-voltage fault management in vacuum.

### 4. Path

1. **MW-scale Microgrid Breadboard:** Hardware-in-the-loop simulation and vacuum testing of a 100 kWh / 100 kW slice of the microgrid architecture to validate fault isolation and thermal management. (Reaches TRL 5).
2. **Subsystem Prototype TVAC:** 0.5 MWh battery bank and 1 MW power conditioning unit tested in a thermal-vacuum chamber under simulated NEA eclipse cycling. (Reaches TRL 6).

### 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk:** Architecture-change.
**Fallback:** Oversize the solar arrays to minimize required storage, accept operational downtime during eclipses, and revert to centralized rather than distributed power conditioning.

### 6. Where others might disagree

Some might argue this is TRL 5 or 6 because it is "just" scaling up ISS batteries or putting terrestrial Megapacks in a vacuum-rated box. This ignores the non-linear thermal management challenges of MWh-class Li-ion storage in a vacuum and the arcing risks of MW-class switching in the space environment.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T20 — Distributed energy storage and microgrid power management

**Current architecture-level TRL: 3–4. Target: TRL 6 before KDP-0B. AD²: 5, rising to 6 if 33,000 substantial-depth cycles are mandatory without replacement.**

The reduced storage requirement makes an Earth-supplied, modular battery architecture plausible. It does **not** establish that an autonomous, megawatt-class NEA power network has been demonstrated. Space battery heritage and terrestrial microgrid heritage support its constituent functions; they do not, by themselves, satisfy the integrated subsystem’s relevant-environment exit criteria.

### Assessment assumptions

- Storage is Earth-manufactured, using qualified rechargeable cells in replaceable, thermally controlled modules. In-space cell manufacture is outside T20.
- Required capacity is **0.5–15 MWh per site**, plus **10–50 kWh per robot**. Whether these are nameplate or end-of-life usable capacities is unresolved.
- Site distribution supplies **2.5–8 MW**; robot tethers operate at **1–3 kV**. Battery strings need not operate directly at tether voltage.
- Vacuum, NEA radiation, microgravity, and the external thermal environment apply to the installed subsystem. Cells may remain within controlled temperature limits; exposing bare cells to asteroid surface temperatures is not a requirement.
- **Service life, discharge power, charging profile, acceptable outage, depth of discharge, and replacement interval remain unspecified.** The proposed **9,000–33,000 cycles** is a contested requirement, not demonstrated performance or an automatic consequence of surface emplacement.
- The obsolete 100 MW, 600 V, SEL4/5 background in rq-0-21/22 is not the assessment baseline.

## 1. Evidence

Ratios below are **required capacity ÷ demonstrated capacity**, unless otherwise specified. They measure scale gaps, not TRL equivalence.

| Heritage and source | Physical demonstration and environment | Scale comparison | What it supports—and does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISS lithium-ion battery replacement programme, NASA, 2017–2021** | Approximately **15 kWh per lithium-ion battery orbital replacement unit**, deployed and operated in orbit in engineered thermal enclosures. | Site capacity: approximately **33–1,000 ORU-equivalents**. Robot capacity: approximately **0.67–3.3 ORU-equivalents**. | Strong flight evidence for rechargeable battery modules, monitoring, protection, and orbital thermal integration. Does not establish NEA lifetime, mining exposure, or autonomous MW-scale network operation. The capacity is approximate; nameplate energy is not guaranteed usable energy. |
| **Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, NASA/JPL, landed 2021** | Two approximately **43 Ah lithium-ion batteries** buffering rover loads; roughly **2.4 kWh combined nominal energy** at approximately 28 V. Successful surface operation in the Martian environment. | Robot capacity: approximately **4–21 times** the combined rover battery energy. | Supports battery-buffered robotic operations and environmental packaging. Mars is not vacuum or microgravity; it does not demonstrate the requested robot capacity, tether interface, or cycle requirement. |
| **Hornsdale Power Reserve, initial installation, South Australia, 2017** | **100 MW / 129 MWh** terrestrial lithium-ion storage system, operated on a utility grid. | Site energy ratio: **0.0039–0.116**; the terrestrial installation is approximately **9–258 times larger**. Site power ratio: **0.025–0.08**, if storage must supply the full site load. | Demonstrates that energy and power scale are not unprecedented on Earth. It does not demonstrate spacecraft packaging, vacuum heat rejection, radiation tolerance, or autonomous NEA fault recovery. |
| **Lasseter et al., “CERTS Microgrid Laboratory Test Bed,” IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics, 2011** | Physical terrestrial microgrid tests with approximately **60 kW-class generating units**, demonstrating local control, islanded operation, and protection concepts. | Site load is approximately **42–133 times one 60 kW unit**. This is a controller-unit comparison, not a claim about total test-bed capacity. | Supports experimentally demonstrated distributed microgrid control principles. It is not evidence for an integrated 1–3 kV DC asteroid network or battery storage subsystem. |

These are programmes and publications I am confident exist. I have **not identified a documented demonstration combining the required battery capacity, MW-scale autonomous management, mining-load interfaces, and NEA-relevant environment**. That absence is the central maturity gap.

## 2. Current TRL and missing exits

### Architecture-level rating: **TRL 3–4**

- **TRL 3 is supported:** battery buffering, modular storage, and distributed power-control critical functions have physical experimental evidence.
- **TRL 4 is conditional:** substantial constituent breadboards exist, but a strict TRL 4 claim for *this integrated subsystem* requires documented laboratory performance against predictions and a documented relevant-environment definition. Neither is supplied here.
- **TRL 5 is not supported:** there is no cited integrated component/breadboard test in the relevant environment with documented scaling requirements covering energy, power, fault isolation, thermal rejection, and lifetime.

The upper bound is therefore not a claim that Project Dyson already has a TRL 4 test article.

| Element | Present assessment at the required application |
|---|---|
| Site battery modules and thermal/protection packaging | **TRL 4–5**, conditional on conservative modular construction and replacement allowance; relevant test evidence for the selected design is still needed. |
| 10–50 kWh robot battery subsystem | **TRL 4–5**; energy scale is reasonably close to space heritage, but mining exposure, transient power, and tether-loss recovery are not demonstrated together. |
| Autonomous MW-class storage/microgrid integration | **TRL 3–4**; terrestrial control results cannot establish space-network readiness. |
| 9,000–33,000-cycle life at unspecified depth of discharge | **Not substantiated.** A separate numerical rating would imply more definition and evidence than presently exist. |

### Requirements that can materially change the assessment

At full site load, ideal energy-only autonomy spans:

\[
t=E/P=0.0625\text{–}6\ \mathrm{h}
\]

That is **3.75 minutes to 6 hours**, before reserve margins, degradation, conversion losses, or temperature effects. A 0.5 MWh bank serving 8 MW would require a nominal **16C** discharge rate if it carries the entire load. Conversely, 15 MWh serving 2.5 MW is approximately **0.17C**. These are radically different storage designs.

Consequently, T20 cannot be treated as merely a capacity procurement problem. Load shedding and critical-load segregation may determine feasibility.

**Metallurgy routes remain separate load cases, not averaged requirements:**

- **No-melt processing:** establish compressor, pumping, heating, and shutdown loads.
- **Rotating smelting:** establish heater power, controlled cooling, rotation continuity, and consequences of interruption.
- **Native-metal/experimentally gated rotating modules:** qualify the actually selected process and its measured transients.

These distinctions concern T20 sizing and protection; they do not assign metallurgy TRLs.

## 3. Target and advancement difficulty

- **0A:** achieve **TRL 4–5 at internal milestones**, with measured load profiles, selected module design, and relevant-environment component tests.
- **0B:** demonstrate **TRL 6 before KDP-0B**, without waiver if safe autonomous power continuity is project-ending.
- **Needed date:** **before KDP-0B authorization**, whose calendar date has not been supplied. The decision date is not a technology-delivery date.
- **Estimated time:** **3–6 years** from funded development and requirements closure, assuming parallel testing and replaceable battery modules.
- **AD²: 5.** A credible development path exists, but the integrated NEA application lacks a directly comparable demonstration.
- **AD² dissent:** **4** is defensible for conservative packaging, limited storage duty, and periodic replacement. **6** is defensible if 33,000 substantial-depth cycles, severe thermal exposure, or no replacement is imposed.

These AD² values use the project’s working anchors, not independently calibrated probabilities of success.

## 4. Advancement path

Costs are **rough-order development estimates in USD**, not vendor quotations. Activities overlap; their durations should not be added mechanically.

| Step | Scale and discriminating result | Cost | Duration | Exit supported |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Requirements and evidence closure** | Define all three process-route load cases; robot loads; outage tolerance; nameplate versus usable capacity; cycle spectrum; radiation and thermal exposure. Validate models against available battery/control test data. | **$0.3–1.0M** | **0.25–0.75 yr** | TRL 3 evidence package and test basis; analysis alone does not establish TRL 4. |
| **Integrated laboratory breadboard** | **10–50 kWh robot pack**, **50–200 kWh site module**, and **100–500 kW** power interfaces; exercise charging, source loss, load shedding, faults, black start, and tether disconnection with representative load hardware. | **$2–6M** | **0.75–1.5 yr** | TRL 4, with performance agreeing with predictions and relevant environment defined. |
| **Relevant-environment module qualification** | Flight-like **10–50 kWh** modules and representative converters: thermal vacuum, radiation testing of sensitive electronics, dust/charging exposure at exposed interfaces, and fault-containment tests. Compare predicted temperatures and electrical behavior with measurements. | **$5–15M** | **1–2 yr** | TRL 5 for tested components, with scaling requirements documented. |
| **Lifetime and degradation campaign** | Multi-cell cohorts and selected modules under the actual depth-of-discharge, temperature, and charging spectrum; validate accelerated-aging models with longer-duration controls. Include failure propagation and protection behavior. | **$3–10M** | **2–5 yr** | Supports TRL 5–6 lifetime evidence; accelerated cycling alone does not establish calendar life. |
| **Integrated relevant-environment prototype** | At least **0.5 MWh**, with **0.5–1 MW** representative power interfaces, autonomous control, realistic communication faults, and flight-like thermal/protection topology. Test representative modules/interfaces in vacuum; correlate the full-network model against physical results and justify extension to 15 MWh/8 MW. | **$15–45M** | **1.5–3 yr** | TRL 6 **only if scaling and environmental equivalence are demonstrated**. Otherwise remains TRL 5. |

A full 15 MWh bank need not fit inside one vacuum chamber. However, modular testing is sufficient only when the scaling argument addresses shared buses, distributed faults, stability, thermal interfaces, and common-cause failures. Hardware-in-the-loop results alone cannot close every environmental gap.

For **rq-0-60**, include the storage-side isolation and converter response to tether arcs or shorts. Tether abrasion and deployment mechanics remain a separate qualification responsibility.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Primary risk class: architecture-change.**

Storage failure need not end 0B if mining and processing can operate intermittently and batteries are replaceable. It becomes **project-ending** if the selected process requires uninterrupted power for safe shutdown or if the adopted autonomy requirement cannot be met by any practical backup arrangement.

**Fallback:** use smaller, replaceable Earth-supplied batteries reserved for controls, communications, safe shutdown, and robot recovery; operate production during available solar power, shed noncritical loads, and abandon continuous-operation requirements.

For smelting, this fallback is acceptable only after experimentally demonstrating a safe interrupted-power sequence. If that cannot be demonstrated, change the processing route or invoke D-02’s **0A-only, Earth-supply** outcome.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Component heritage versus integrated readiness.** A rating of 6–9 may be offered because space batteries have flown and terrestrial storage exceeds the required capacity. That is valid heritage attribution, but not the revised subsystem’s demonstrated TRL.
2. **TRL 3 versus 4 today.** This is the strongest legitimate disagreement. I retain 3–4 because no Project Dyson integrated breadboard evidence was supplied.
3. **Cycle life.** Shallow daily buffering and deep, repeated outage bridging are different requirements. Neither the cycle count nor the necessary depth is settled.
4. **What counts as relevant environment.** Thermally controlled modules reduce the cell qualification burden, but do not eliminate vacuum thermal rejection, radiation, exposed-interface charging, or network integration.
5. **Risk classification.** Architecture-change is the baseline; project-ending is appropriate if continuous power is an indispensable process-safety requirement.

# T20 Consolidated Rating: Distributed Energy Storage and Microgrid Power Management

*Rapporteur's note: This consolidates three assessments. Divergences are preserved and attributed. Where this note compares figures across models, it reports what each model said. It adds no independent technical judgement.*

---

## 1. Summary table

| | **Claude Opus 5.5** | **Gemini 3.1 Pro** | **GPT-6.1 Sol** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scope treatment** | Split into three elements: T20-R robot packs, T20-S site storage, T20-P 1–3 kV MW microgrid | Single integrated rating | Single integrated architecture rating, with element sub-ratings |
| **Current TRL (headline)** | **3–5** | **3–4** | **3–4** |
| Element ratings | R: 4–5 · S: 4–5 · P: 3–4 | — (battery chemistry and 10–50 kWh packaging called TRL 9) | Site modules 4–5 · Robot 4–5 · MW integration 3–4 · Cycle life "not substantiated" (deliberately unrated) |
| **AD²** | **4** (5 if 15 MWh at ≥30k cycles becomes the reference) | **4** | **5** (dissent range: 4 for conservative/replaceable, 6 for 33k deep cycles with no replacement) |
| **Target at KDP-0B** | **5** for S and P; **6** for R; **6** for S and P by 0B PDR. Rises to 6 at KDP-0B if surface arrays plus continuous furnace are adopted | **6** | **6** (0A internal milestones: 4–5) |
| **Risk class** | Architecture-change. Cost-increase if stand-off arrays are already the reference. Near project-ending under continuous furnace on a slow rotator | Architecture-change | Architecture-change. Project-ending if continuous power is a process-safety requirement |
| **Years to target** | 3–6 | 2–4 | 3–6 |
| **Self-stated confidence** | Medium | High | Medium |
| **Related RQs** | rq-0-60 only. Explicitly excludes rq-0-21 and rq-0-22 as superseded | rq-0-21, rq-0-22, rq-0-60 | Lists rq-0-21, rq-0-22, rq-0-60, while stating that the 21/22 background "is not the assessment baseline" |
| **Sum of listed step costs** (rapporteur arithmetic; steps overlap) | ~$38–116M including the pathfinder increment; ~$18–56M excluding it | ~$20–50M | ~$25–77M |

---

## 2. Where the models agree

1. **TRL floor is 3.** All three set the lower bound at 3, and all locate it in MW-class integration or microgrid management rather than in battery cells.
2. **Cell and module heritage is strong, but integrated readiness is not.** All three hold that flight-proven Li-ion modules (ISS) do not by themselves establish readiness for an MWh-class NEA microgrid. Each explicitly rejects the "it's just paralleling ISS batteries / Megapacks in a box" argument for TRL 5–6:
   - Claude §6.2
   - Gemini §6
   - GPT §6.1
3. **The gaps are thermal and fault behaviour in vacuum at scale.** All three identify these as the core unmet items: vacuum heat rejection, high-voltage arcing and fault isolation at kV / MW, and integrated testing.
4. **Baseline risk class is architecture-change.** All three agree. Claude and GPT both name conditions under which it escalates to project-ending, specifically continuous-power or furnace process routes.
5. **Phase need is 0B.**
6. **Fallbacks converge.** Each fallback reduces storage to critical or keep-alive loads and accepts intermittent production:
   - Claude: keep-alive ≤1.5 MWh plus nightly curtailment
   - Gemini: accept eclipse downtime
   - GPT: critical loads only, intermittent operation

   Claude and GPT both name D-02's "0A only, Earth supply" as the terminal fallback.
7. **Terrestrial MWh-to-GWh storage is not environment-relevant evidence.** All three agree, whichever example is cited.
8. **rq-0-60 (tether insulation) bears on T20 through the robot power interface.** All three agree.

---

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

### D1. TRL ceiling: 4 versus 5

- **Positions:**
  - Claude: headline ceiling 5, driven by its R and S element ratings.
  - Gemini: ceiling 4, stated as unmet.
  - GPT: architecture ceiling 4, described as conditional.
- **Why:** This is largely an **aggregation-method difference**, not an evidence difference. Claude's and GPT's element ratings for site modules and robot packs are identical (4–5). They differ only on whether the headline reflects the best element or the integrated subsystem.
  - GPT states that its TRL 4 is "conditional" because no integrated breadboard or documented relevant-environment definition was supplied.
  - Gemini says TRL 4 is unmet because no MWh bank and MW controller have been tested together in vacuum.
- **Justification of the lower bound differs:**
  - Gemini rests TRL 3 on "analytical models of MW-class space power systems".
  - Claude and GPT rest it on physical test data: terrestrial MVDC/microgrid tests and ISS EPS (Claude); experimental evidence of the critical functions (GPT).
  - GPT separately states that "analysis alone does not establish TRL 4".
- **What would settle it:**
  - A panel decision on whether T20 is rated as one item or as separate elements.
  - Documented existence (or absence) of an integrated laboratory breadboard whose performance matches predictions.

### D2. Target at KDP-0B: 5 versus 6

- **Positions:**
  - Claude: 5 for S/P at KDP-0B, 6 by PDR.
  - Gemini and GPT: 6 at KDP-0B.
- **Why:** The models interpret D-02 differently given the risk class.
  - Claude argues that T20 is not project-ending if a fallback exists, so D-02 does not mandate TRL 6 at KDP-0B. Claude concedes the target should rise to 6 under surface arrays plus Gemini's continuous furnace.
  - GPT ties 6 "without waiver" to the case where autonomous power continuity is project-ending.
  - Gemini states 6 is needed for the 0B site power architecture, without a D-02 argument.
- **What would settle it:**
  - Selection of the reference metallurgy route and array siting.
  - A determination of whether uninterrupted power is a process-safety requirement. GPT proposes an experimental safe interrupted-power sequence for smelting.
  - A KDP-0B calendar date. None was supplied; Claude assumes about 2031–2033.

### D3. AD²: 4 versus 5 (with stated band 4–6)

- **Why:** The models depend on different requirement assumptions.
  - Claude and Gemini rate 4 on the basis that similar development has been done (ISS EPS, terrestrial microgrids).
  - GPT rates 5 because no directly comparable integrated NEA demonstration exists.
  - Both Claude and GPT state that the rating moves (to 5, or to 6) if deep, high-count cycling without replacement becomes the reference.
- **What would settle it:** Requirements closure on cycle count, depth of discharge (DoD) and replacement interval.

### D4. Years to target: 2–4 versus 3–6

- **Why:** The paths differ in content.
  - Gemini's two-step path contains no lifetime or degradation campaign and no requirements-closure step.
  - Claude and GPT both include multi-year cycle-life testing. Claude gives 2–6 years and notes that real-time 33k cycles at a 4 h period takes 15 years; GPT gives 2–5 years.
- **What would settle it:**
  - Agreement on whether TRL 6 requires lifetime evidence, or only TVAC and integration.
  - The cycle requirement itself (see D5).

### D5. The 9,000–33,000-cycle requirement and whether heritage meets it

- **Positions:**
  - **Gemini** treats the range as a requirement and states that ISS ORUs, "designed for ~60,000 LEO cycles over 10 years", exceed it.
  - **Claude** says the figure is conditional on surface-sited arrays and is consistent with a 4–10 h rotation over 10–15 years, but states it has not seen the derivation. Claude notes the binding requirement becomes outage energy and power if arrays are stand-off.
  - **GPT** calls it "contested" and says the required DoD is undefined, so it declines to rate cycle life.
- **Why:** Claude and GPT both stress that cycle capability depends on DoD; Gemini's comparison does not address DoD.
- **What would settle it:**
  - Documentation of the ISS ORU cycle-life specification and the DoD it assumes.
  - Requirements closure on siting, rotation envelope, DoD and the curtail-versus-ride-through choice.

### D6. Storage sizing and mass closure (raised only by Claude, partly by GPT)

- **Claude** gives its own arithmetic and labels it "not data", contestable by roughly ±30–50%:
  - Night length about 1–5 h.
  - Full ride-through needs 2.5–40 MWh.
  - The 15 MWh high end could reach about 600–700 t installed, exceeding one tug payload.
- **GPT** gives energy-to-power autonomy of 3.75 min to 6 h, and C-rates from 16C (0.5 MWh at 8 MW) to 0.17C (15 MWh at 2.5 MW). It concludes these are "radically different storage designs".
- **Gemini** does not address sizing or mass.
- **Not a dispute on evidence.** This is an unaddressed requirement question. It would be settled by requirements closure and a verified space-pack specific-energy figure (Claude's 100–150 Wh/kg is its own unverified estimate).

### D7. Dependence on metallurgy route

- Claude and GPT both treat the three metallurgy routes as separate load cases.
  - Claude maps them to storage size: no-melt goes low, rotating furnace goes high or toward thermal storage.
  - GPT gives each route distinct load and shutdown questions.
- Gemini does not distinguish routes.
- Only Claude proposes a thermal-storage alternative for furnace standby.

### D8. What test reaches TRL 6 for site storage

- **Gemini:** a 0.5 MWh / 1 MW subsystem in TVAC.
- **GPT:** at least 0.5 MWh with 0.5–1 MW interfaces, plus vacuum-tested *representative modules* and a correlated scaling model to 15 MWh / 8 MW. GPT states TRL 6 is earned "only if scaling and environmental equivalence are demonstrated".
- **Claude:** even the pathfinder leaves MWh "extrapolated by ~10–100×". Site storage and microgrid therefore reach only "partial 6" by that route; Claude's own S/P TRL 6 is placed at 0B PDR.
- **What would settle it:** A panel ruling on the acceptable scaling argument for modular site storage, meaning what fraction of full scale must be tested, and in what environment.

### D9. Fallback detail

- **Only Gemini:**
  - oversize the solar arrays;
  - revert to *centralized* power conditioning.
- **Only Claude:**
  - restrict target selection to fast rotators;
  - stand-off or co-orbiting arrays. Claude notes this creates a new transmission technology to rate.
- **Only GPT:** smelting curtailment is acceptable only after a demonstrated safe interrupted-power sequence.

### D10. Confidence

Gemini rates its own assessment high; Claude and GPT rate theirs medium.

---

## 4. Evidence register

| Evidence | Cited by | Figures given | Flags |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISS Li-ion ORU replacement (2017–2021)** | All three | **Gemini:** ~9.7 kWh per ORU, 24 ORUs, ~300 kWh total, ~60,000-cycle design. **GPT:** ~15 kWh per ORU. **Claude:** aggregate "order 10² kWh", ~16 cycles/day | ⚠ **Per-unit capacity conflicts** (9.7 vs ~15 kWh); Claude marks its aggregate *unverified* and the claim *confident: false*. This drives different scale ratios. Robot: Gemini "1:1" vs GPT 0.67–3.3. Site: Gemini 50:1, GPT 33–1,000, Claude ~2–100. Separately, Gemini's own 9.7 kWh figure sits below the 10–50 kWh robot range it calls a "perfect match". ⚠ The 60,000-cycle spec is **Gemini only**. ⚠ Claude's claim text says "MW-scale cycling heritage" while its demonstrated scale is ~10² kWh, so the entry is internally inconsistent. **Settle with:** NASA / ORU specification documentation |
| **Mars rovers (Curiosity 2012–; Perseverance 2021–)** | Claude (both rovers); GPT (Perseverance) | Two batteries of ~42–43 Ah, ~2–3 kWh (Claude) / ~2.4 kWh at ~28 V (GPT). Robot ratio ~4–20× / ~4–21× | Consistent between the two. Claude is "mostly" confident on Ah. Both note Mars is not vacuum |
| **ISS EPS DC microgrid** | Claude; Gemini | Claude: 160 V primary / 120 V secondary, ~0.1 MW. Gemini: ~120 kW. Power ratio ~25–80× (Claude), ~65:1 (Gemini) | Broadly consistent |
| **Hubble NiH₂ batteries (1990–2009)** | **Claude only** | ~19 yr, ~10⁵ shallow-DoD cycles, ~10 kWh class | ⚠ Energy figure "from memory"; Claude unsure of it |
| **Apollo 15–17 LRV radiator dust** | **Claude only** | Failure-mode precedent | ⚠ Claude marked unsure; no specific document cited |
| **GEO high-voltage array arcing (Hoeber et al., AIAA, 1998)** | **Claude only** | ~100 V-class arrays | ⚠ Claude marked the citation unverified |
| **Moss Landing BESS (~3 GWh class; fire January 2025)** | **Claude only** | Terrestrial | Capacity "approximately"; existence and fire confident |
| **Hornsdale Power Reserve (100 MW / 129 MWh, 2017)** | **GPT only** | Terrestrial | Confident |
| **Tesla Megapack** | **Gemini only** | "1–100 MWh", ratio "1:1 (but not in space environment)" | Generic product citation, no specific installation |
| **Lasseter et al., CERTS Microgrid Laboratory Test Bed, IEEE Trans. Power Electronics, 2011** | **GPT only** | ~60 kW-class units; site ~42–133× one unit | Confident; the only peer-reviewed microgrid-control citation given |
| **Li-ion partial-DoD ageing data (LFP/NMC)** | **Claude only** | Lab cells | Class-level, no specific paper cited |
| **Negative evidence:** no flown flywheel or regenerative fuel cell at relevant scale (ISS flywheel did not fly) | **Claude only** | — | "To my knowledge" |
| **Excluded as non-evidence:** rq-0-21/22 and the attached literature review | Claude (explicit); GPT (as "not baseline") | — | Claude also flags the review's "$100–300/cm²" cell cost as possibly an order of magnitude high, but says it has not verified this. Gemini lists the RQs without comment |

**Strongest common evidence:** ISS Li-ion ORUs (all three) and ISS EPS (two models). The models agree on what this evidence shows qualitatively but **disagree on its quantitative scale**. That disagreement should be resolved before scale ratios are recorded.

---

## 5. Consolidated path

Steps are merged where the models propose equivalent activities. Attribution and cost ranges are preserved as given. Activities overlap in time.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Requirements closure:** siting (surface vs stand-off), rotation and night envelope, curtail vs ride-through per metallurgy route, outage and tether-cut cases, discharge power, nameplate vs usable capacity, cycle spectrum and DoD | Claude; GPT (not in Gemini) | Site-level, all routes | 0.2–0.8M (C) / 0.3–1.0M (G) | 0.5–1 yr (C) / 0.25–0.75 yr (G) | TRL 4 enabler (C); TRL 3 evidence package only (G) |

| 3 | **Integrated laboratory breadboard:** robot pack, site module, 100–500 kW interfaces; faults, black start, load shedding, tether disconnect | GPT; Gemini (100 kWh / 100 kW, *in TVAC*) | 10–50 kWh + 50–200 kWh, 100–500 kW (GPT); 100 kWh / 100 kW (Gemini) | 2–6M (GPT) / 5–15M (Gemini) | 0.75–1.5 yr / 1–2 yr | TRL 4 (GPT); TRL 5 (Gemini) |
| 4 | **Vacuum HV arc / Paschen tests at 1–3 kV with charged simulant,** including storage-side isolation response to tether arcs or shorts (shared with rq-0-60) | Claude; GPT (storage-side response) | Components | 1–3M (C) | 1–2 yr | TRL 4 for T20-P (C) |
